sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- lens_diagnostics: lens_diagnostics source=session reads the session cache and an empty cache is not proof of a clean file; use source=lsp scope=paths for changed files when cached findings are absent or stale
- symbol_search: Find files by identifier
- effective_config: Explain resolved configuration
- project_report: Orient in a project before choosing a file
- module_report: Outline a source module before reading a body
- read_symbol: Read one symbol's body instead of the whole file
- read_enclosing: Read the enclosing symbol or callback body for a line
- pi_lens_activate_tools: Activate a situational tool
- subagent_gate: Run subagent tasks with bounded retries and a required success quorum
- workspace_session_summaries: Inspect same-CWD session summaries before potentially overlapping repository work
- subagent: Delegate focused work to child agents; compose multi-child work in one workflow call.
- subagents_enable: pi-subagents is installed. For authorized specialist, independent-review, or parallel work, call subagents_enable, then subagent. Authorization must come from the current request or applicable instructions; complexity alone is not authorization.
- ask_user_question: Ask the user up to 4 structured questions (2-4 options each) when requirements are ambiguous
- workflow: Delegate substantive independent or staged work to subagents with a JavaScript workflow, optionally composing agent calls with parallel(), pipeline(), or both
- workflow_control: Inspect and manage workflow runs directly by canonical run ID.

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use subagent_gate instead of raw subagent calls when a delegated result must be retried safely or a success quorum must be enforced.
- Set each subagent_gate task retrySafety to read-only only when rerunning it cannot duplicate file mutations or external side effects; omission defaults to may-write.
- Use workspace_session_summaries when another Pi session in the same working directory may overlap the current work.
- After workspace_session_summaries, compare goals, files or symbols, decisions, and next steps; when overlap is material or ownership is unclear, coordinate through intercom before writing.
- Use ask_user_question whenever the user's request is underspecified and you cannot proceed without concrete decisions — you can ask up to 4 questions per invocation.
- Each question MUST have 2-4 options. Every option requires a concise label (1-5 words) and a description explaining what the choice means or its trade-offs. The user can additionally type a custom answer via the automatically appended "Type something." row on every question, or press Esc to abandon the questionnaire. Do NOT author "Other" or "Type something." labels yourself — reserved labels are rejected at runtime.
- Set multiSelect: true when multiple answers are valid. Provide an options[].preview markdown string when an option benefits from richer side-by-side context (mockups, code snippets, diagrams, configs) — single-select only. The "Type something." row is appended to every question; in preview mode it expands to the full pane width while typing so the custom answer is not cramped into the narrow options column. If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option and append "(Recommended)" to its label.
- Do not stack multiple ask_user_question calls back-to-back — group all clarifying questions into one invocation.
- The `workflow` tool runs multi-agent orchestration — it fans decomposable work out across subagents, and fits tasks shaped like: repo-wide inspection, independent parallel research/checks, multi-perspective review, or fan-out/fan-in synthesis. ONLY call it when the user explicitly opts in — via the workflow trigger word, `/workflows run`, or their own words (e.g. 'run a workflow', 'fan this out', '并行审一遍'). For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit — do not call it; you may briefly offer it (with a rough cost) as an option instead.
- Use workflow_control for workflow lifecycle management; do not ask the user to type /workflows when this tool can perform the action.
- Use stop to terminate or quit a run. Closing the navigator does not stop a run.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.description: Run a JavaScript workflow that delegates work to subagents with agent(), optionally composing calls with parallel() and pipeline().

Add phases: [{ title: 'Phase' }] only when the workflow has named phases, and declare only phases it will use. With multiple phases, call phase('Exact Title') before each phase's work or set `phase` in the agent options. Use `await workflow(savedName, childArgs)` to run a saved workflow inline; nesting is limited to one level and shares the parent run's concurrency, agent, and token limits. Optional quality helpers include verify(), judgePanel(), loopUntilDry(), and completenessCheck(). Optional control helpers include retry() and gate(); budget exposes total, spent(), and remaining(), and phase('Name', { budget: N }) sets a phase token limit. The optional `agentType` option selects a named user or project definition that can bind tools, a model, and role instructions; use it only when its name and purpose are provided in context. Its bound model overrides `tier`; an explicit `model` overrides both. Use plain JavaScript only; imports, require(), filesystem modules, Date.now(), Math.random(), and new Date() are unavailable. Use phase('Name'), agent(prompt, opts), parallel(arrayOfFunctions), pipeline(items, ...stages), log(message), args, cwd, process.cwd(), and budget. The workflow must call agent() at least once. parallel() requires functions, not promises, and returns results in input order: await parallel(items.map(item => () => agent(...))). pipeline(items, ...stages) runs stages sequentially for each item while items proceed concurrently; each stage receives (previousValue, originalItem, index).

# Values

## User understandable over technical language

I feel like code should always be understandable by users as they are the ones who dictate process. So the goal of code should make it the most understandable with zero context as possible

### Principles

- Long variables names where needed to be descriptive
- Avoid using technical language such as “factory” or “barrel”
- Stick to a common language profile, (tasks always being tasks, stages always being stages etc)
- File structure should reflect the call stack
- Use of JSDocs to explain variables in pure english
- Include why things are done not just what is done
- Use a labelled data inport pattern (IE  `({varA , varB}) => {}`)
- NEVER MENTION DESIGN PATTERNS
- Use @example tags in js doc to easily explain functionality
  
  

## Functional over Object oreintated

Although pure functional code can tend to insanity it is always important to note co-mingle state and functionality. Where possible state should leave in clearly defined places, and functions should show a clear line in how we move from one state to another. Traditional object oriented design mainly serves to gatekeep devs(or for game dev).

### Principles

- Try and avoid using classes where possible
- Currying can be used to create sudo classes, avoid that
- Functions should follow black box mentality, clear input delivers the same output with no side affects
- Treat variables as immutable unless they are clearly defined states.
- Functions should always be named with a verb in, as they are doing something
- Give the miniumn data to each function as possible. Pick off fields before invocation.
- Each function should only work to achieve its task, with a single responsibility


## Co-location over abstraction

Although abstraction is an essential part of coding it should always only be done by business level intent, not just on functionality. Ideally if you pick a random file in the codebase you should only need to look at the one folder above it and one folder under it to get all the context on its functionality.

### Principles
- Unit tests should always be placed next to the relevant file
- Generally functions called in a higher function should be placed in a folder of that functions name. IE if `funA.js` calls `funB.js` it should be `./funA/funB.js`
- Generic/helper functions should only be made if they are repeatedly doing the same thing.
- Helpers should be treated like react state and exist at the lowest level folder that is common in the hierarchy of the folders
- If abstracting it would take up more lines/characters than just embedding that line directly on a per file basis avoid doing it. IE don’t abstract a single line just because its repeated unless it has some complex logic like a regex.
- Don’t fear repetition of code
- Make sure the code is easily searchable for any given task. If I said modify the task history box in the ui it should  be easy and logical to figure out where that is.
- Use folders as a tool for organising

## Tested over trusted 

Functionality should not assumed to exist until it is tested and evidenced. “it should work” isn’t always reliable and we want to make sure there are no regressions. 

### Principles
- Try and at least plan what tests you are going to make before you  code a function
- Don’t assume typing is correct until proven, or allow it to fail safe
- Failures should clear transparent and observable, every function doesnt need to intensly check it just needs to report failures accurately
- Tests must be consistent
- Integration test must reflect how a user could want to use the app
- Use the lowest possible level of tests( Ie Unit over api over e2e) for the fastest test cycle


## Fast iteration over long planning

Sometimes you just can’t know what will happen without using it and that is essential. Spending too long planning can cause ideas to get confused or get you trapped in a loop where you just make plans worse.  Having simple clear checkpoints is great.

### Principles
- When planning, factor in points to check certain things and how the plan can be adapted when needed
- Try and create safe ways to test functionality, ie not in prod, when possible as this will allow you to confirm things work.
- Focus on one small change at a time, get tests passing then work on the next element.
- Always design code with the intent it will be changed/replaced soon
- Minimise friction in development even if it is small
- Make change easy, then make the change. Even if making change easy is hard.



# Inspirations
My principles here are inspired by:

- Extreme programming Explained by Kent Beck (book)
- Life isn’t binary (book)
- Intent driven design by David whitney (Talk)


# Examples

## Intent Driven descriptions

### Bad Example

```js

const userInOneYearFactory = (name, age, users) => {

    const user = {name: name , age: age + 1}

    users.push(user)
  
}

const list = []

userFactory("Frank",32,list)


```

## Good example

```js

/**
* MARK: calculateAgeNextYear
* @description calculates the age someone will be next year
* @example const usersAgeNextYear = calculateAgeNextYear({ageNow: 3})  
console.log(usersAgeNextYear) // 4
*/
const calculateAgeNextYear = ({ageNow}) => {
  const ageNextYear = ageNow + 1
  
  return ageNextYear
}

const userObjectsList = []

const usersName = "Frank"
const usersAge = 32

const usersAgeNextYear = calculateAgeNextYear({ageNow: usersAge})

userObjectsList.push({name: usersName, age: usersAge})


```

## 1. Current architecture (verified in this repo)

How a Runner gets work today (all paths read during planning):

1. **Stages** live on the project/workflow and are normalized additively in [api/project/stageNormalizers.js](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/api/project/stageNormalizers.js): `normalizeStage` / `normalizeStages` only touch `skills`, `tags`, `harness`, `runOnBranch`/`customBranch` when present, so legacy stages round-trip byte-identically. New optional fields follow the same present-only pattern. The stage editor UI is [frontend/src/components/workflow/StageSettingsDrawer.jsx](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/frontend/src/components/workflow/StageSettingsDrawer.jsx); the pause/fallback section at the bottom (lines ~146–215) is the natural neighbor for the new control. [frontend/src/components/workflow/StageTagEditor.jsx](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/frontend/src/components/workflow/StageTagEditor.jsx) is the closest "list editor in this drawer" precedent to copy.
2. **Dispatch scan** (`POST /runners/dispatch` in [api/flow/runnerRoutes.js](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/api/flow/runnerRoutes.js)): [api/flow/dispatch/scanClaimableTasks.js](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/api/flow/dispatch/scanClaimableTasks.js) finds candidate tasks, [api/flow/dispatch/taskRequirements.js](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/api/flow/dispatch/taskRequirements.js) derives `{ harness, model, tier, alias, runnableType, kind, stageId }`, then each candidate is tested with [api/flow/dispatch/runnerMatches.js](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/api/flow/dispatch/runnerMatches.js). Misses are loud reason codes aggregated into the `NO_CAPABLE_MATCH` response.
3. **Runner-side operator settings** are enforced in one shared helper, [api/flow/dispatch/operatorConfigVerdict.js](/home/server/.kainbain/runner-work/kb-a3753643-7aa5-49da-8201-4499615200b6/api/flow/dispatch/operatorConfigVerdict.js), called from **three** paths so no claim route bypasses it: the dispatch scan (via `runnerMatches`), direct claim (`POST /tasks/:id/claim`, verdict at `runnerRoutes.js:839`), and merge-lease acquire (`POST /runners/integration/acquire`, verdict at `runnerRoutes.js:1209`). This is the pattern to copy: one pure verdict helper, called from every claim path.
4. **Runner identity** is the `runnerId` string. A repo-wide search confirms there is currently **no `runnerPolicy`/`allowedRunners`/`blockedRunners` code anywhere**, and **no runner labels/tags infrastructure** (no `labels` on records, facts, capabilities, or `operatorConfig`) — labels would be new Runner-advertise + backend-store/match plumbing on both sides.
5. **What is Runner-runnable (correction to stale comments):** the `taskRequirements.js` docblock still says "only agent/review … human, command, and ci stages stay embedded", but the code (lines 34–41) says otherwise: post-DA9 every command stage is Runner-runnable (`hostCommand` is always `false`, `hostOnly` is stripped in `normalizeStage`), and `runnableType` is true for `agent`, `review`, `ci`, **and `merge`**. 6. **The merge path is the awkward one:** `POST /runners/integration/acquire` currently enforces with only `{ kind: "merge" }` and no stage context (`runnerRoutes.js:1209-1212`), so a stage allow/block list for merge stages requires resolving task→stage there (or explicitly scoping merge out of v1 — see D6).

- A **stage-centric** rule (stage names which runners may take it) is the mirror image of the existing **runner-centric** `operatorConfig` (runner names which projects/tools it serves). It needs its own verdict helper but the same "one enforcement point, called from every claim path" discipline.

| # | Survey question | Recommended default | Why |

New miss reason (e.g. `RUNNER_NOT_ALLOWED`) + monitor visibility. Manual recovery stays via existing operator moves, not a new bypass. |
| q4 | Stage-only, or also project/group defaults? | **Stage-only in v1** | The task asks for stage settings. Project defaults add precedence rules (stage vs project) for unclear value; note as follow-up. |
| q5 | Who can edit the lists? | **Anyone who can already edit stage settings** | No permission system exists for stages; inventing one is out of scope. |
| q6 | Who sets runner labels? (conditional on labels) | **Admin-managed, centrally** (when labels land) | The compliance use case ("must run onsite") is meaningless if the runner self-declares its labels. Self-reported labels are spoofable; operator-owned labels in `operatorConfig` are enforceable. |

If any survey answer comes back differently, only the flagged decision (D1–D6 in §4) changes; the phase order is unchanged. Re-check §2 before starting Phase 3.

## 3. Approach: make the change easy, then make the change

**Make the change easy (Phases 0–2, behavior-preserving):**

- P0: timeboxed research spikes that retire the two unknowns (merge-lease stage resolution; runner-picker data availability) before any code is shaped around them.
- P1: introduce the shared stage-runner-policy module + fixtures with **no wiring** (pure functions, fully tested, nothing calls them yet).
- P2: plumb stage/policy context to the one claim path that lacks it (integration acquire) in a behavior-preserving way, or formally scope merge out with a recorded decision.

**Make the change (Phases 3–6):**

- P3: data model + normalization + persistence round-trip.
- P4: enforcement on all claim paths + loud miss reasons.
- P5: UI at the bottom of stage settings.
- P6: observability, docs, rollout/verification.

Each phase lands as a reviewable unit with its own tests; P0–P2 are safe to land even if the feature is later rescoped.

## 4. Key design decisions

- **D1 — Storage shape.** `stage.runnerPolicy = { mode: "allow" | "block", runners: [<runnerId>, …] }`, entirely optional/absent = unrestricted. Empty `runners` array = unrestricted regardless of mode (fail-open, never strand tasks on a mis-edit). Additive normalization in `normalizeStage` (trim, drop non-strings/blanks, dedupe) mirroring the `tags` pattern. Reject unknown `mode` at the API boundary with 400, but never reject unknown runnerIds (see D4). Reserve sibling key space for a future `labels` extension rather than overloading `runners`.
- **D2 — Enforcement point.** New pure helper `stageRunnerPolicyVerdict(stageOrPolicy, runnerId, …)` in `api/flow/dispatch/` (sibling to `operatorConfigVerdict.js`), returning `{ ok, reason }` with loud codes (`RUNNER_NOT_ALLOWED` / `RUNNER_BLOCKED`). `taskRequirements()` attaches the current stage's policy to `req`; `runnerMatches()` enforces it **after** health/capability gates (stable reasons keep priority — a stale runner still reports `STALE_HEARTBEAT`) and alongside `operatorConfigVerdict`. Direct claim and integration-acquire routes call the same helper so no path bypasses it. Decide and document the order of the two verdicts (operator vs stage) and test the combined case.
- **D3 — No fallback execution.** A restricted stage with no eligible runner waits (q3). No silent reroute, no auto-fail. The stuck/stall surfacing must distinguish "waiting for an allowed runner" from generic idleness (see P6).
- **D4 — Name matching.** Exact `runnerId` match (trimmed). Unknown/deleted runnerIds in a policy are kept (not auto-pruned) and shown as stale in the UI, so renaming a runner never silently opens a compliance gate. Renames are an operator action with a visible warning.
- **D5 — Human/non-runnable stages.** Policy is stored but inert for `human` stages (`runnableType: false` — never dispatched). UI may still show the control for consistency, with a note that it only affects runner-dispatched work.
- **D6 — Merge stages in v1.** Preferred: enforce on the merge path too (publish/merge is a motivating example; code path exists via `cand.stage` on the dispatch merge branch). Cost: `POST /runners/integration/acquire` must resolve task→stage to get the policy. If P0.2 shows that resolution is invasive, fallback is: v1 covers agent/ci; merge-lease enforcement is a fast follow with the same helper. Record whichever is chosen before P4.

## 5. Work plan (ordered; big pieces / research first)

### Phase 0 — Research spikes (no production code; timeboxed)

- **0.1 Dispatch-path audit.** Confirm the full set of execution paths a policy must cover by re-reading `runnerRoutes.js` dispatch/claim/lease routes plus `scanClaimableTasks.js` and scheduler deferral counters. Output: a short note listing every claim path a stage policy must gate, or proof that claim-path enforcement is sufficient.
- **0.2 Merge-path stage resolution spike.** Find the cheapest correct way to get from `POST /runners/integration/acquire` (`projectId` + `targetBranch`) to the task's current stage policy. Options: (a) look up the queued task in `integrationQueue` by project+branch, (b) require `taskId` in the acquire body, (c) enforce only at dispatch time (the dispatch route already has `cand.stage`) and treat direct acquire as operator-trusted. Output: chosen option + estimate; feeds D6.
- **0.3 Runner-picker data check.** Confirm `GET /runners` returns everything the stage-settings picker needs (id + displayName + status). If display names are missing for some records, the picker falls back to runnerId — no backend change.

### Phase 1 — Make the change easy: shared policy module (no wiring)

- **1.1** Create `api/flow/dispatch/stageRunnerPolicy.js` (pure): `normalizeStageRunnerPolicy(raw)` + `stageRunnerPolicyVerdict(policy, runnerId)`. Fail-open on absent/malformed input (legacy-safe, like `operatorConfigVerdict`). ## Stage Runner access

Every stage has an optional **Runner access** list at the bottom of its settings. It restricts which Runners may take that stage — without blocking a whole category of work:

- **Off (every Runner)** *(default)* — no restriction; any capable Runner takes the stage.
- **Only these runners** — an allow list: e.g. only the one Runner that can publish to remote takes the `Publish` stage.
- **All except these runners** — a block list: e.g. a legal-compliance scan runs only on onsite Runners by blocking the cloud ones.

The list names Runners by their Runner id (shown with display names where set). An empty selection means unrestricted, and a save with an unknown mode is refused with a 400 naming the stage — a typo can never silently save as unrestricted. Runner ids that no longer register stay in the list with an "unknown" badge instead of being pruned, so renaming a Runner never silently opens the gate; removing them is explicit.

Enforcement covers every claim path: Runner dispatch, direct task claims, and merge leases all refuse ineligible Runners (dispatch reports `RUNNER_NOT_ALLOWED` / `RUNNER_BLOCKED` in its miss histogram; claims and leases answer 409). A restricted stage with no eligible Runner waits — it never fails or reroutes. This stage-side list applies **in addition to** each Runner's own operator settings (System Settings › Runners: project scope, job-type switches, tool filter) — both gates must pass. Human stages run no Runner work, so the list does not affect them.

Enforcement covers every claim path: Runner dispatch, direct task claims, and merge leases all refuse ineligible Runners (dispatch reports `RUNNER_NOT_ALLOWED` / `RUNNER_BLOCKED` in its miss histogram; claims and leases answer 409). A restricted stage with no eligible Runner waits — it never fails or reroutes. This stage-side list applies **in addition to** each Runner's own operator settings (System Settings › Runners: project scope, job-type switches, tool filter) — both gates must pass. Human stages run no Runner work, so the list does not affect them.

## Stage change badges

Each history row's `+N -M` badge measures that stage's own commit range (stage start → stage end on the task branch), not the whole task branch. An editing stage keeps its real counts; a testing stage that changes nothing shows `+0 -0`. When a stage fails, its partial work is committed with a `... (failed)` message first, so the failed attempt owns its own diff and a retry measures only the retry. Rows recorded before this scheme (no range data) render exactly as before.

## Task statuses

A task's `status` tells you where it stands: `idle`, `in_stage`, `waiting_human`, `running_agent`, `running_ci`, `advancing`, `checkpoint`, `blocked`, `paused`, `interrupted`, `failed`, `passed`, `completed`. (Old records may still carry the legacy `running_deploy` label, which reads as `running_ci`.)

## Driving a task

- **Execute** runs the current stage (`POST /tasks/:id/execute`).
- **Advance** approves a checkpoint and moves on; optional guidance is appended to the goal. Approving a last-stage checkpoint completes the task instead (the UI says "Approve & Mark Complete").
- **Reject** sends it back with required human feedback.
- **Failback / move / jump** route a task to an earlier or arbitrary stage.
- **Retry** re-runs a failed stage with a freshly curated prompt; **pause/resume** and **abort** control live execution.

Auto-iteration can re-run a failed stage automatically (fix, re-test, re-review) up to a configured limit before parking the task as `failed` for a human.

## Retry budgets

Every failed stage consumes from two loop budgets: the **auto-iteration budget** (failback-and-retry cycles) and the **transient budget** (same-stage retries for timeouts and infrastructure errors). Budgets resolve per stage as **stage override → project override → global default**; a project-wide value lives in Project Settings › Retry & Timeouts (Project tab), and a per-stage value (when set) still wins over both. A budget of `0` disables that loop; a blank project field follows the global default.

Hitting **retry** (`POST /tasks/:id/retry`, the failed-stage banner button) gives the task a genuinely fresh attempt: both loop counters restart at zero and the stage clock re-enters, so the next failure auto-retries again instead of parking immediately. The parking failure is still reinjected into the retried attempt's prompt as context. Plain **execute** (`POST /tasks/:id/execute`, the Run Stage button) is first-run/manual dispatch — it keeps counting from the current values and never restarts a budget, so the scheduler can never silently grant infinite retries.
